View in browser                 Greg Ip   The Oil Shock Could Make Us Stronger   Plus, AI in science, bias in prediction markets, and Alan Greenspan’s crisis handbook   The oil shock brought on by the war with Iran has ravaged truckers, angered voters and endangered Republicans’ control of Congress.

   Here’s the surprise: It may be making the economy stronger.

   The reason is the oft-forgotten fact that the U.S. is a net petroleum exporter. When war disrupts the supply of oil and gas from other countries, the U.S. reaps a double benefit: more market share, and higher prices. This is a reason, though not the only one, that growth is not just solid but may be accelerating .

   In a new paper, Diego R. Känzig and Luca Zanotti of Northwestern University and James H. Stock of Harvard show that before 2010, activity such as unemployment and industrial production generally got worse after an oil shock, whereas since 2010, activity improved . The reason, they surmise: the shale-oil revolution, which turned the U.S. from a net importer of 12 million barrels a day into a net exporter of more than 3 million barrels.

         They find the economic boost comes not through increased exports, but from higher prices for U.S. exports (in economics, better “terms of trade”), which translate into higher profits, wealth and incomes, more than offsetting the harm to consumers’ purchasing power from inflation.

   Their analysis doesn’t extend to this year’s war with Iran, but Känzig said in an interview he expected its effects to be more benign or even positive compared with pre-2010 shocks.

   The flip side of the record diesel prices paid by farmers, truckers and factories are steep margins for refiners. Energy companies’ profits doubled in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to FactSet. Their shares are up more than tech stocks. There’s a reason the industry lobbied so fiercely , and successfully, against a federal diesel-export ban.

   Oil shocks used to have persistent effects on inflation and thus interest rates. The authors find interest rates still go up—but partly for good reasons, i.e., better growth. That’s one reason the Federal Reserve’s pivot to tighter policy hasn’t bothered the stock market.

Examining a sample of about 225,000 recent dissertations in technical fields, Duke University’s Daniel Gross and two co-authors find that AI writing, nearly absent from dissertations filed three years ago, is now found in about 30% . Scientists and engineers who don’t use AI tend to be in higher-ranked programs (just 9% of MIT dissertations appeared to use AI), and are also more likely to stay in academia after graduation. 

   Prediction markets don’t seem to tilt left or right. Eric Zitzewitz of Dartmouth studied pre-election bets from 1880 to the present (long before digital markets, major newspapers used to publish odds), and found no evidence that markets overprice candidates of either party. In recent U.S. races, there is also no bias by age, race or gender. One apparent bias: Betting markets tend to overrate underdogs. So think twice before betting on that long shot.

   Did tariffs really slash imports from China? U.S. data shows them down 26% from 2024, but they are only down 4%, using Chinese data on exports to the U.S., Gregory Auclair of the Peterson Institute notes. A potential explanation: tariff evasion , perhaps through dishonest reporting or rerouting goods through third-party countries. For example, the U.S. reports far higher imports from Vietnam than exports reported by Vietnam to the U.S.

   Greenspan’s financial-crisis playbook. Former Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke, at a memorial to his predecessor, Alan Greenspan, that I attended on Sept. 28: “When Alan first became chair he had the foresight to be worried about the possibility of a financial crisis so he had the staff draw up a variety of contingency plans. Then the stock market fell 23%. But nothing ever happens as expected and the planning was no help at all. When I became chair I found Alan’s plans and had them extended and expanded. Crisis came. No help at all.”

The Oil Shock Could Make Us Stronger
 
Plus, AI in science, bias in prediction markets, and Alan Greenspan’s crisis handbook
 

The oil shock brought on by the war with Iran has ravaged truckers, angered voters and endangered Republicans’ control of Congress.

 

Here’s the surprise: It may be making the economy stronger.

 

The reason is the oft-forgotten fact that the U.S. is a net petroleum exporter. When war disrupts the supply of oil and gas from other countries, the U.S. reaps a double benefit: more market share, and higher prices. This is a reason, though not the only one, that growth is not just solid but may be accelerating.

 

In a new paper, Diego R. Känzig and Luca Zanotti of Northwestern University and James H. Stock of Harvard show that before 2010, activity such as unemployment and industrial production generally got worse after an oil shock, whereas since 2010, activity improved. The reason, they surmise: the shale-oil revolution, which turned the U.S. from a net importer of 12 million barrels a day into a net exporter of more than 3 million barrels.

 
 
 
 

They find the economic boost comes not through increased exports, but from higher prices for U.S. exports (in economics, better “terms of trade”), which translate into higher profits, wealth and incomes, more than offsetting the harm to consumers’ purchasing power from inflation.

 

Their analysis doesn’t extend to this year’s war with Iran, but Känzig said in an interview he expected its effects to be more benign or even positive compared with pre-2010 shocks.

 

The flip side of the record diesel prices paid by farmers, truckers and factories are steep margins for refiners. Energy companies’ profits doubled in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to FactSet. Their shares are up more than tech stocks. There’s a reason the industry lobbied so fiercely, and successfully, against a federal diesel-export ban.

 

Oil shocks used to have persistent effects on inflation and thus interest rates. The authors find interest rates still go up—but partly for good reasons, i.e., better growth. That’s one reason the Federal Reserve’s pivot to tighter policy hasn’t bothered the stock market.

What I’m Following

 

High-achieving young scientists rely less on AI than more average researchers. Examining a sample of about 225,000 recent dissertations in technical fields, Duke University’s Daniel Gross and two co-authors find that AI writing, nearly absent from dissertations filed three years ago, is now found in about 30%. Scientists and engineers who don’t use AI tend to be in higher-ranked programs (just 9% of MIT dissertations appeared to use AI), and are also more likely to stay in academia after graduation. 

 

Prediction markets don’t seem to tilt left or right. Eric Zitzewitz of Dartmouth studied pre-election bets from 1880 to the present (long before digital markets, major newspapers used to publish odds), and found no evidence that markets overprice candidates of either party. In recent U.S. races, there is also no bias by age, race or gender. One apparent bias: Betting markets tend to overrate underdogs. So think twice before betting on that long shot.

 

Did tariffs really slash imports from China? U.S. data shows them down 26% from 2024, but they are only down 4%, using Chinese data on exports to the U.S., Gregory Auclair of the Peterson Institute notes. A potential explanation: tariff evasion, perhaps through dishonest reporting or rerouting goods through third-party countries. For example, the U.S. reports far higher imports from Vietnam than exports reported by Vietnam to the U.S.

 

Greenspan’s financial-crisis playbook. Former Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke, at a memorial to his predecessor, Alan Greenspan, that I attended on Sept. 28: “When Alan first became chair he had the foresight to be worried about the possibility of a financial crisis so he had the staff draw up a variety of contingency plans. Then the stock market fell 23%. But nothing ever happens as expected and the planning was no help at all. When I became chair I found Alan’s plans and had them extended and expanded. Crisis came. No help at all.”
